references.text: The anointed priest brings the blood to the tent of meeting; the same procedure is repeated for the sin of the entire congregation of Israel.
On the Day of Atonement, the priest takes blood from the bull and brings it into the sanctuary, a similar ritual involving blood.
Moses anoints Aaron with anointing oil, making him the anointed priest (הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ).
The consecration of priests involves bull's blood at the tent of meeting; the same sanctuary and sacrificial animal are mentioned.
The tent of meeting (אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד) is mentioned as the place where the Lord meets with His people.
A sin offering in which the blood is brought into the tent of meeting must be burned, not eaten.
Christ, as high priest, entered the sanctuary with His own blood, fulfilling the Old Testament blood sacrifice.
The high priest enters the second room with blood for himself and for the people's sins, parallel to the action of the anointed priest.
Completion of the ritual where the carrying of the blood into the tent (v.5) leads to atonement and forgiveness (v.20).
Contrasting ritual practice: the blood of the burnt offering is sprinkled on the altar at the entrance, while the blood of the sin offering is carried into the tent.
A theological contrast showing that for common sins the blood remains on the altar, whereas the priest must bring it into the tent.
